newsitem.title: USA: U.S. congressman predicts North Korean apology.
newsitem.headline: U.S. congressman predicts North Korean apology.

text.p: Democratic Representative Bill Richardson, who met with North Korean officials earlier this week, predicted on Friday that Pyongyang soon would issue an apology to end the dispute over a submarine that ran aground in South Korea in September.
The New Mexico congressman, who is a close confidant of President Bill Clinton, dismissed as "rhetoric" a new warning from North Korea to the United States not to side with the South.

"My impression is that within the next two weeks the North Koreans will make a statement of regret because they know that they have got an awful lot to lose," Richardson said in an interview on the PBS programme "Newshour with Jim Lehrer."

Richardson, who negotiated the release this week of a young American detained in North Korea for three months on espionage charges, said officials in the communist state asked him to stay an extra day to dicuss the submarine dispute and other issues "they wanted to get off their chest."
He called Pyongyang's renewed warnings to Washington "provocative," but added: "I think that's rhetoric. That's press rhetoric. North Koreans negotiate like this. They feel it gives them leverage."

Tension has remained high on the divided Korean peninsula since a submarine landed 26 North Koreans off South Korea's eastern city Kangnung in September. Twenty-four of the intruders were shot to death, one was captured and the other is still missing.
South Korea has demanded that Pyongyang apologise but North Korea has instead demanded the return of the vessel, the captured crewmember and the bodies.
Richardson said he thought North Korea realised it had made "a terrible mistake" with the submarine incident and the detention of 26-year-old American Carl Hunziker on spying charges.

Hunziker was arrested in North Korea near the border with China on Aug. 24 when he swam across the Yalu River separating the two countries. Richardson described him as "a confused young man, good intentions, very idealistic" and said Hunziker had strayed into North Korea "in an adventuresome frolic."

"I think they (North Korea) realised unless they released Hunziker, unless they made some kind of admission of error and contrition over this submarine incident ... that unless they put those issues behind them, the United States and the international community was going to continue being leery of them," the congressman said.
The United States, Richardson said, also wanted to put the Hunziker incident to rest so that dialogue on on reducing tensions in the region could go forward.
"But there's no question that unless North Korea makes a statement of regret or contrition on the submarine incident, a lot of progress is going to be derailed," he added.

The Hunziker release was the second time in two years that Richardson had helped gain the freedom of an American held in North Korea. In December, 1994, he helped negotiate the release of U.S. helicopter pilot Bobby Hall who was shot down when he strayed into North Korean air space.
